course.title: Electronics Foundations
course.description: Work out how simple direct-current circuits behave, using diagrams you can change and calculations you can check.
course.audience: A beginner using an Arduino starter kit or studying introductory electricity.

paragraphs: A 9 V battery, a 450 Ω resistor and a wire joining them make the simplest working circuit, and what flows in it can be calculated from two numbers: the current is 9 divided by 450, which is 0.02 A. The same arithmetic, extended a step at a time, describes torches, phone chargers and every board in an Arduino starter kit, and it explains why a part burns out when it is asked to carry more than it was made for.

The course has five lessons, each resting on the one before, and all of them use low-voltage direct current from a battery or a USB supply. The first follows the current round a single loop and arrives at Ohm's law; the next two add a second resistor, first one after the other and then side by side; the fourth turns to the energy a circuit moves each second, which decides how hot a part becomes; and the last looks at parts such as the LED that do not obey Ohm's law, ending with the resistor that keeps an LED safe.
Each lesson explains an idea first, works one example through, and then asks you to do the same, so numbers are part of the work and a calculator is worth keeping nearby.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the current in a loop from its voltage and resistance, using Ohm's law.
You'll be able to find the total resistance of a series circuit and the voltage across each part.
You'll be able to find the current in each branch of a parallel circuit and its equivalent resistance.
You'll be able to work out the power of a component and the energy it transfers in a given time.
You'll be able to choose the resistor that sets the current through an LED.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with decimals and division; no electronics is assumed.

lessons.title: Current in a single loop

steps.headline: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point

lead.text: A metal wire is full of electrons that are free to drift along it, and each electron carries a very small amount of negative **electric charge**. Charge is counted in **coulombs**, and because a single electron carries only about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, one coulomb is the charge of roughly 6.2 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

What a circuit does depends on how quickly that charge moves past a point, and not only on how much of it there is, so the quantity that matters is called **current**. It is the charge passing a point in one second: if 2 coulombs pass in 4 seconds the current is 2 ÷ 4, which is 0.5 coulombs each second. A current of one coulomb each second has a unit of its own, the **ampere** (A), named for the French physicist André-Marie Ampère, and so this current is written 0.5 A.

Because current is a *rate* of flow, the meter that reads it, marked A, has to be placed in the wire itself so that all the flow passes through it. The next screen uses two such meters to compare the flow at different points of one loop.

steps.headline: A single loop carries the same current at every point

lead.text: Follow the wire in the figure from one terminal of the battery. It passes through a meter, then through the **resistor**, a component made to hold the flow back, then through a second meter, and finally returns to the other terminal, with no side route anywhere along the way. A loop of this kind has a single path, and it must be unbroken before anything flows, since a gap at any point stops the flow at every point.

Both meters read 0.1 A. No charge can leave the wire inside the resistor, and none is created there, so the charge entering it each second is the charge leaving it each second, and **the current after the resistor equals the current before it**. The resistor limits how much flows round the loop as a whole, but it does not use any of the current up.

The arrows run from the positive terminal of the battery round to the negative one, a direction known as *conventional* current. Benjamin Franklin fixed the labels positive and negative in the eighteenth century, before anyone knew what moves in a wire, and the electron was identified only in 1897 by J. J. Thomson, after which it became clear that the electrons in a wire drift the opposite way. The convention has stayed because the calculations give the same results whichever way the arrows point, as long as one direction is used throughout.

lead.text: Before the second meter is read, apply what the last screen showed about a loop with a single path. The first meter, placed just before the resistor, gives one reading, and the question is what the second will give.

reveal.text: The second meter reads exactly what the first did. The resistor decides how large the current is for the loop as a whole, and the first meter already shows that, but it removes none of the flow as the charge passes through, so a meter placed anywhere on the loop gives the same reading.

steps.headline: Voltage is the push that drives the current

lead.text: [[Charge|What electrons carry, counted in coulombs. Met in 'Current is the rate at which charge passes a point'.]] does not begin to move of its own accord, and in a circuit the push comes from the battery. A battery keeps its two terminals at different electrical levels, and the difference between them is its **voltage**, measured in **volts** (V), a unit named for Alessandro Volta, who built the first electric battery in 1800. A 9 V battery pushes harder than a 1.5 V cell, and a USB port supplies 5 V.

Voltage is always a difference between two points, which is why it is measured *across* a component, with a probe at each end, and not through it. In the loop in the figure the battery supplies 5 V, and since the resistor is the only component joined between the terminals, the resistor has the whole 5 V across it.

Current is what flows round the loop, whereas voltage does not *flow* at all: it is the difference that drives the flow. With the same resistor in the loop, a larger voltage drives a larger current, and a smaller voltage a smaller one, so the two rise and fall together.

steps.headline: Resistance is how strongly a part holds the current back

lead.text: Two parts joined to the same battery do not necessarily carry the same current. A short, thick copper wire lets a great deal through, while the thin metal filament of a lamp lets through far less, and the property that accounts for the difference is called **resistance**. It is measured in **ohms**, written with the Greek capital letter omega (Ω), and the *larger* the resistance, the more strongly the part opposes the [[current|The charge passing a point each second, measured in amperes. Met in 'Current is the rate at which charge passes a point'.]].

In the figure the battery supplies 5 V. With a 100 Ω resistor the current is 0.05 A, and when that resistor is replaced by one of 250 Ω, which is 2.5 times as large, the current falls to 0.02 A, which is 2.5 times as small. The battery is the same in both cases, so the difference comes from the part.

It is tempting to picture a resistor as soaking up current, but it behaves like the narrow neck in the pipe at the start of the lesson: it limits how much can flow round the whole loop and keeps none of it back. **Resistance sets how much current a given voltage can drive**, and the next screen makes that relationship exact.

steps.headline: Ohm's law: the current is the voltage divided by the resistance

lead.text: Georg Simon Ohm measured this relationship in metal wires in the 1820s and published it in 1827, and it can be written as a single equation, **I = V ÷ R**, in which I is the current in amperes, V is the voltage in volts and R is the resistance in ohms. The equation is called **Ohm's law**, and it puts the voltage on top of the division and the resistance underneath.

The figure shows three loops. A 9 V battery across 90 Ω gives 9 ÷ 90, which is 0.1 A. Doubling the voltage to 18 V across the same 90 Ω gives 0.2 A, so the current *doubles* with the voltage, while keeping 9 V and doubling the resistance to 180 Ω gives 9 ÷ 180, which is 0.05 A, so the current is *halved*.

Placing the resistance underneath is what makes a larger resistance give a smaller current, and the units agree, since volts divided by ohms leave amperes. The law describes ordinary resistors, whose resistance stays the same whatever the voltage across them, and the last lesson of this course meets parts that do not behave in this way.

steps.headline: Finding the current for 9 V across 450 Ω

lead.text: A 9 V battery is joined across a single 450 Ω resistor, and [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Ohm's law: the current is the voltage divided by the resistance'.]] gives the current, with the units kept beside the numbers.

workedSteps.text: Write the law first, so that the quantity to be found stands alone on the left.
Put the battery voltage on top and the resistance underneath, each with its unit.
Divide, and the volts divided by ohms leave amperes.

steps.headline: Finding the current for 6 V across 150 Ω

lead.text: The next loop has 6 V across 150 Ω. The first two lines are set out as before, and the last one is yours.

workedSteps.text: Start from the same equation.
Put 6 V on top and 150 Ω underneath.
Divide, and give the current in amperes.

lead.text: This time the whole calculation is yours, starting from the equation. The loop is the one whose meters read 0.05 A earlier in the lesson, so the answer can be compared with what the meters showed.

reveal.text: 5 ÷ 100 is 0.05, so the current is 0.05 A, which is what both meters read earlier. Ohm's law and the meters agree because the law is a description of exactly what the meters show.

lead.text: Ohm's law also says which changes to a loop raise the current and which lower it, without any arithmetic. Look at what each change does to the number on top of the division and to the number underneath it.

reveal.text: Only a higher supply voltage raises the current. A second resistor along the same path, a larger resistor and a longer wire each add to the resistance, which sits underneath in I = V ÷ R, so each of them lowers the current.

lead.text: The last loop needs both ideas from the lesson: Ohm's law gives the current, and the single path then fixes what a meter placed anywhere along it will read.

stageTitles.review: Recall what a single loop does

blocks.text: Take a closed loop of pipe with a pump in one side of it, and let the water circulate. If you count the litres that pass a mark on the pipe in one second, and then count them again at a mark beyond a narrow neck, the two counts agree, because the loop is full and the water arriving at the neck has nowhere to go except through it. The neck does limit how much the pump can move round the whole loop, since a narrow pipe holds the flow back everywhere at once, but **at any moment the same amount passes every mark**.

A battery joined by wire to a single component makes a loop of the same kind, with the battery in place of the pump and the wire in place of the pipe. What circulates in it cannot be seen, yet a meter placed in the wire can count it, and the readings behave just as the litre counts do, which is the first thing this lesson sets out to show.

It matters because every circuit later in this course, however many parts it has, is built from loops like this one. Once you can say how much flows round a single loop, given the battery and the part in it, you can also say whether a part from an Arduino kit will cope with a given supply, and that decision separates a circuit that works from one that burns out a component.

lessons.title: Resistance in series

steps.headline: Resistors joined end to end share one current

lead.text: In the figure the wire leaves the battery, passes through a 100 Ω resistor and then through a 200 Ω resistor, and returns to the battery with no side route anywhere along it. Parts joined in this way, one after the other on a single path, are said to be in **series**.

Each of the two meters reads 0.03 A. The argument is the one from the last lesson, applied twice: charge cannot collect between the resistors or leave the wire there, so the charge passing the first resistor each second goes on to pass the second, and **the current is the same through every part in series**, whatever the resistors are.

It is tempting to expect the [[current|The charge passing a point each second, measured in amperes. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] to be weaker after the larger resistor, as if the first part had taken some of it. A resistor does not take current from the loop, though; it limits how much the loop can carry at all, so both resistors and the wire between them carry the *same* amount. Why that amount is 0.03 A, a third of the current in the single 100 Ω loop, is the subject of the next screens.

lead.text: The 200 Ω resistor holds the flow back twice as strongly as the 100 Ω one, so it is natural to wonder whether the two meters should differ. Use what the last screen said about parts in series.

reveal.text: Both meters read 0.03 A. The larger resistor neither makes more charge pass nor uses any up; its larger resistance only means that it takes a larger share of the battery's voltage, which a later screen works out.

steps.headline: Resistances in series add to a total

lead.text: Charge in the loop has to pass through each resistor in turn, so each one adds its *own* opposition to that of the others, and the loop holds the flow back as a single resistor of the **total resistance** would. The total is the sum of the separate resistances, R = R₁ + R₂, and a third resistor simply adds a third term. In the figure, 100 Ω and 150 Ω together make 250 Ω, and a further 200 Ω raises the total to 450 Ω.

Once the total is known, [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] applies to the whole loop exactly as it did to one resistor. With a 9 V battery, 250 Ω gives 9 ÷ 250, which is 0.036 A through every part, and 450 Ω gives 9 ÷ 450, which is 0.02 A, so **each resistor added to the path lowers the current**.

It follows that the total is always larger than the largest single resistance, since nothing in the chain can cancel what the others hold back. The loop that opened the lesson shows it: 100 Ω and 200 Ω make 300 Ω, and 9 ÷ 300 is the 0.03 A that the meters read, a third of the 0.09 A that the 100 Ω resistor allowed alone.

steps.headline: The voltage across a resistor is the current times its resistance

lead.text: With the current known, [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] can be *turned round* to give the voltage across a single resistor. Since I = V ÷ R, multiplying both sides by R gives **V = I × R**. In the figure the current is 0.03 A, so the 100 Ω resistor has 0.03 × 100, which is 3 V across it, and the 200 Ω resistor has 0.03 × 200, which is 6 V.

The voltage across one part of a loop is called its **voltage drop**, because the electrical level falls by that amount from one side of the part to the other as the current passes through. The two drops are not equal: the 200 Ω resistor has twice the drop of the 100 Ω one, since the same current meets twice the resistance.

The current must therefore be found first, from the total resistance, before any drop can be found. A common mistake is to divide the battery voltage by one resistor alone, which gives the current that resistor would carry on its own, and not the smaller current it carries in the loop.

steps.headline: The voltage drops add up to the battery voltage

lead.text: In the figure the [[voltage drops|The voltage across one part of a loop, equal to the current times its resistance. Met in 'The voltage across a resistor is the current times its resistance'.]] are 3 V and 6 V, and together they come to 9 V, the voltage of the battery. This is required and not accidental: the battery raises the electrical level by 9 V, and by the time the current has gone right round the loop the level must be *back* where it began, so **the drops must add up to the battery's voltage**. The rule was first stated by Gustav Kirchhoff in 1845, while he was still a student, and it is known as Kirchhoff's voltage law.

Each resistor takes a share in proportion to its resistance. With 100 Ω and 200 Ω the resistances are in the ratio 1 to 2, and so are the drops, 3 V and 6 V, while a 6 V battery across the same pair gives 0.02 A and drops of 2 V and 4 V, which again add up to the battery's voltage.

The rule also gives a shortcut. If the battery voltage and one drop are known, the other drop is whatever remains, so with 6 V across the pair and 2 V across the first resistor, 6 − 2 leaves 4 V for the other, with no need to find the current at all.

blocks.text: A 9 V battery joined across a single 100 Ω resistor drives 0.09 A. If a second resistor of 200 Ω is added, so that the wire runs from the battery through one resistor and then through the other, the current becomes 0.03 A, only a third of what it was. The new resistor has changed the current everywhere in the loop, including in the resistor that was there already, and **the size of the change can be predicted exactly**.

Nothing needed for the prediction is new: one path still means one current, and [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] still ties the current to the voltage and the resistance. What is new is the question of how two resistances act together on that one current, and how the battery's voltage is divided between the two parts, and both answers follow from the two earlier ideas.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add resistances in series, find the current they allow, and work out how the battery's voltage divides between them.

recap.keyIdea: Resistors in series carry one current, their resistances add, and the battery's voltage divides between them in proportion to their resistances.

blocks.text: In a series loop the [[current|The charge passing a point each second, measured in amperes. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] is the same through every part, and the resistances add to a total, so that I = V ÷ R applies to the whole loop with **the total resistance underneath**. The voltage across each resistor is then its own resistance times that current, and these *drops* add up to the voltage of the battery, with the larger resistance taking the larger share.
Because the drops must add up to the battery's voltage, knowing all but one of them gives the last at once, which lets a loop of several resistors be worked through one step at a time.

lessons.title: When a circuit splits into branches

steps.headline: Branches joined across the same two points each get the full voltage

lead.text: In the figure a 6 V battery has a 20 Ω resistor connected across its two terminals. A second resistor of 30 Ω is then connected across the same two terminals, and a third of 60 Ω across them again. Each resistor forms a separate route for the charge, called a **branch**, and branches connected in this way are said to be in **parallel**.

Every branch begins at one terminal of the battery and ends at the other, so all the branches have the same two points at their ends, and the voltage between two points does not depend on which route is taken between them. **Every branch therefore has the full battery voltage across it**, 6 V in each case however many branches are added, provided that the connecting wires have negligible resistance.

This is the opposite of a [[series|Parts joined one after the other on a single path, which therefore share one current. Met in 'Resistors joined end to end share one current'.]] loop, in which the same *current* passes every part and the voltage is divided between them. Here the voltage is the same for every part, and what differs from one branch to another is the current, as the next screens show.

reveal.text: Each lamp is connected between the same two battery terminals, so each has the full 6 V across it, and the voltage across one lamp is not changed by the presence of the other.

steps.headline: Each branch carries the supply voltage divided by its own resistance

lead.text: Because every branch has the full voltage across it, [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] applies to each branch on its own: the current in a branch is the supply voltage divided by that branch's resistance. In the figure a 12 V battery across a 40 Ω branch gives 12 ÷ 40, which is 0.3 A.

When a 120 Ω branch is connected across the battery as well, it carries 12 ÷ 120, which is 0.1 A, and the first branch stays at 0.3 A, because its voltage and its resistance have not changed. A branch has no way of detecting the others, so **adding a branch never changes the current in the branches already there**.

The branch with the larger resistance carries the smaller current, in inverse proportion: 120 Ω is three times 40 Ω, and 0.1 A is a third of 0.3 A. In a parallel circuit the voltage is the same for every branch, and it is the *current* that differs.

steps.headline: The battery supplies the sum of the branch currents

lead.text: Follow the wire from the battery in the figure. It reaches a **junction**, a point where wires meet, and there the current divides, part of it going into the 40 Ω branch and part into the 120 Ω branch, before the two parts meet again at a second junction and return together to the battery.

Charge cannot collect at a junction, and none is created there, which is the same reasoning as in a single loop, so the charge arriving each second must equal the charge leaving each second. The battery therefore supplies 0.3 A + 0.1 A = 0.4 A, **the sum of the branch currents**, and the wire carrying 0.4 A splits into 0.3 A and 0.1 A at the first junction and recombines at the second.

The single-loop rule survives in a modified form, then: the current is the same at every point *along one route*, but the current in the main wire is shared out between the routes. More branches draw more current from the battery, which is why too many appliances on a single supply can overload its wiring.

lead.text: A 12 V supply is connected across a 100 Ω branch and a 300 Ω branch. The two branch currents are set out, and the total is yours.

workedSteps.text: The 100 Ω branch has the full 12 V across it.
The 300 Ω branch has the same 12 V across it.
The supply provides both, so add the two currents to find the total in amperes.

steps.headline: Two branches can be replaced by one equivalent resistor

lead.text: From the battery's side the whole arrangement is a single load that draws a total current. In the figure a 12 V battery supplies 0.4 A to the 40 Ω and 120 Ω branches, and it would supply exactly the same current to a single resistor of the right size. That size follows from [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] applied to the battery's voltage and the total current: 12 V ÷ 0.4 A is 30 Ω, and a resistor of this value, which can stand in for the branches without changing what the battery supplies, is called their **equivalent resistance**.

The 30 Ω is smaller than either branch, and this is no accident. Each new branch gives the charge another route, so the battery supplies *more* current than before and the resistance it faces falls. In a series loop the total grew with every part, whereas here the equivalent resistance shrinks with every branch.

The equivalent resistance is therefore always less than the resistance of the branch with the smallest resistance, since that branch alone already draws its current and every other branch only adds to it.

lead.text: The last screen gave a rule for the size of the equivalent resistance that needs no arithmetic. Apply it to a 50 Ω branch and a 200 Ω branch before the number is worked out.

reveal.text: The equivalent resistance is below 50 Ω, and the rule on the next screen gives it as 40 Ω. Whatever the second branch is, even a very large resistance, it can only add a route and so can only lower the equivalent resistance.

steps.headline: The reciprocal rule gives the equivalent resistance directly

lead.text: The equivalent resistance can be found without knowing the battery's voltage at all. Each branch carries V ÷ R, so the total current is V ÷ R₁ + V ÷ R₂, and the equivalent resistance R must satisfy V ÷ R = V ÷ R₁ + V ÷ R₂. The voltage V appears in every term and cancels, which leaves **1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂**.

The fraction 1/R is the **reciprocal** of the resistance, so the rule says that the reciprocals of the branch resistances add, and that the sum is turned over to get back to ohms. For the 40 Ω and 120 Ω branches, 1/40 + 1/120 is 3/120 + 1/120, which is 4/120, or 1/30, so R is 30 Ω, in agreement with the 12 V ÷ 0.4 A found from the battery.

Two equal branches are the simplest case: 1/100 + 1/100 is 2/100, so two 100 Ω branches give 50 Ω, and in general *n* equal branches give one n-th of a single branch. For a 50 Ω branch and a 200 Ω branch, 1/50 + 1/200 is 4/200 + 1/200, which is 5/200, or 1/40, and so the equivalent resistance is 40 Ω.
The rule is easiest to apply when the two branches are equal, because the two reciprocals are then the same fraction.

reveal.text: 1/100 + 1/100 is 2/100, which is 1/50, so the equivalent resistance is 50 Ω. Two equal branches halve the resistance of one, because the battery supplies twice the current from the same voltage.

lead.text: The last circuit asks for a total current, which can be reached through the branch currents or through the equivalent resistance. Both routes give the same answer.

blocks.text: Take a 6 V battery and a 20 Ω resistor, which together carry 0.3 A. If a second 20 Ω resistor is added in series, as in the last lesson, the resistance doubles to 40 Ω and the current falls to 0.15 A. If the second resistor is instead joined with one end on each terminal of the battery, so that it forms a route of its own, the first resistor still carries 0.3 A exactly as before and the battery now supplies 0.6 A. **The same resistor, added in two different ways, lowers the current in one case and raises it in the other.**

The difference lies in the connection and not in the part, and the connection is what this lesson examines. Charge now has a choice of routes, so the rule that served for a single path, one current everywhere, no longer applies, and its replacement is built from the one thing that stays the same, which is the voltage across each route. Houses are wired in this second way, which is why switching on a second lamp does not dim the first.

Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] gives each branch its own current, the supply voltage divided by that branch's resistance. The battery supplies the *sum* of the branch currents, and adding a branch leaves the others unchanged while raising the total.

The single resistance that would draw the same total current from the battery is the equivalent resistance, found from 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂, and it is always smaller than the resistance of the smallest branch.

lessons.title: How much energy a circuit moves

steps.headline: A volt is one joule of energy for each coulomb

lead.text: A battery does work on the charge that passes through it, and the energy involved is counted in **joules** (J), a unit named for James Prescott Joule, who showed in the early 1840s that the heat produced by a current depends on the current and the resistance. The energy is *carried* round the loop by the charge and transferred to whatever part the current passes through, where it appears as heat or light.

The voltage of a battery tells how much energy it gives to each [[coulomb|The unit of electric charge. Met in 'Current is the rate at which charge passes a point'.]] of charge: **one volt is one joule for each coulomb**. In the figure a 4 V battery gives each coulomb 4 J, drawn as four squares, and a 9 V battery gives each coulomb 9 J. A part with 9 V across it likewise receives 9 J from every coulomb that passes through it.

How much energy arrives each second therefore depends on a second thing as well, which is how many coulombs pass in that second. That is exactly what the current counts, since an ampere is one coulomb each second, and the next screen puts the two together.

reveal.text: Half a coulomb passes each second and each coulomb carries 4 J, so the battery delivers 0.5 × 4 = 2 J every second.

steps.headline: Power is the rate of energy transfer, and P = I × V

lead.text: Energy each second is a rate, like the current, and it has a name of its own: **power**. Its unit is the **watt** (W), which is one [[joule|The unit of energy. One volt is one joule for each coulomb. Met in 'A volt is one joule of energy for each coulomb'.]] each second, named for James Watt. A part with a voltage V across it receives V joules from each coulomb, and I coulombs pass each second, so the energy it receives each second is I × V, and **P = I × V**.

In the figure, 0.2 A at 5 V gives 0.2 × 5, which is 1 W. Doubling the voltage to 10 V gives 0.2 × 10 = 2 W, and doubling the current to 0.4 A at 5 V gives 0.4 × 5 = 2 W, so the power rises in step with *either* quantity.

Small currents in electronics are often given in **milliamperes** (mA), where one milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere, so that 20 mA is 0.02 A. The current has to be converted to amperes before it is multiplied by the voltage in volts, because otherwise the answer is not in watts.

steps.headline: With Ohm's law, power can be found from the resistance

lead.text: Often the current or the voltage across a resistor is unknown while its resistance is given, and [[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] supplies the missing quantity. Since V = I × R, putting I × R in place of V in P = I × V gives **P = I²R**, and since I = V ÷ R, putting V ÷ R in place of I gives **P = V² ÷ R**. These are one power written in different terms, and which form to use depends only on which two quantities are known.
A 20 Ω resistor carrying 0.3 A has 0.3 × 20 = 6 V across it, so P = 0.3 × 6 = 1.8 W. The other forms agree: I²R is 0.09 × 20 = 1.8 W, and V² ÷ R is 36 ÷ 20 = 1.8 W.

The squares have a consequence. Doubling the voltage across a resistor doubles the current as well, so the power rises *fourfold* and not twofold, and this is the reason why a small increase in supply voltage can matter more than it seems.
Choose the form of the relation that uses the two quantities the question gives, and keep the units beside the numbers.

reveal.text: V² ÷ R is 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 W. Finding the current first, 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05 A, and then multiplying by 5 V gives the same 0.25 W, since the two forms are one relation.

steps.headline: A resistor turns the power it receives into heat

lead.text: In a resistor the energy transferred becomes heat, and the resistor warms until it loses heat to the air as fast as it receives it. Every resistor therefore has a **power rating**, the greatest [[power|The energy transferred each second, in watts. Met in 'Power is the rate of energy transfer'.]] it can transfer without damage, and the small resistors of a starter kit are commonly rated at 0.25 W.

The figure puts a 100 Ω resistor on two supplies. With 3 V across it, V² ÷ R is 9 ÷ 100, which is 0.09 W, comfortably below the 0.25 W rating. With 9 V across it, V² ÷ R is 81 ÷ 100, which is 0.81 W, more than three times the rating, and the resistor would overheat.

Tripling the voltage raised the power *ninefold*, because the current tripled as well, so a part that is safe on one supply can fail on another that looks only a little larger. The calculation is how a part is checked against its rating before it is connected.

steps.headline: Energy is power multiplied by time

lead.text: Power gives the joules transferred each second, so the energy transferred over a stretch of time is the power multiplied by the time, **E = P × t**, with E in joules, P in watts and t in seconds. The graph shows a 5 W lamp, which transfers 5 J every second and so has transferred 50 J after 10 s.

A 0.9 W lamp is a gentler load, and its line rises more slowly, reaching 0.9 × 30 = 27 J after 30 s. The steeper the line, the greater the power, and the time must be in seconds for the energy to come out in joules, so a minute is 60 s and an hour is 3600 s.

Power and energy are easily confused, but power is how *fast* energy is being transferred and energy is how *much* has been transferred. A high power for a short time and a low power for a long time can transfer the same energy, which is why electricity is sold by the kilowatt-hour, an energy of 3.6 million joules, and not by the watt.

blocks.text: A resistor of the common small kind in an Arduino kit is rated for 0.25 W, and a 100 Ω resistor of this kind can be connected to a 3 V supply or to a 9 V supply, but not with equal safety. On 3 V it stays barely warm, whereas on 9 V it receives nine times as much energy each second and can become too hot to touch, although its resistance is the same in both cases. **Tripling the voltage did far more than triple the heating.**

What decides whether a part survives is neither the voltage nor the current taken alone, but the energy the circuit moves through the part each second, and that follows from the two taken together. Once it can be calculated, a part can be checked against its rating before it is connected, and the energy a lamp transfers over a given time can be found as well.

intro.promise: By the end you'll calculate the power of a component in watts, check it against a rating, and find the energy it transfers over a given time.

recap.keyIdea: Power is the energy transferred each second, found from the current and voltage as P = I × V, and the energy over a time is the power multiplied by that time.

blocks.text: One volt is one joule for each coulomb, and a current is a number of coulombs each second, so [[Power|The energy transferred each second, in watts. Met in 'Power is the rate of energy transfer'.]] in watts is the current times the voltage, **P = I × V**. With Ohm's law the same power can be written P = I²R or P = V² ÷ R, whichever uses the quantities that are known.

In a resistor the power becomes heat, which is why a part has a *rating* that its power must not exceed, and over a time t the energy transferred is **E = P × t**, in joules when the time is in seconds.

recap.nextHook: Every part so far has followed Ohm's law, and the last lesson looks at parts that do not, and at the resistor that keeps one of them safe.

lessons.title: Components that break the pattern

steps.headline: An ohmic part has a straight-line graph through the origin

lead.text: In the graph each dot is a measurement of the current in a 50 Ω resistor at one voltage: 0.02 A at 1 V, 0.04 A at 2 V, 0.06 A at 3 V and 0.08 A at 4 V. The dots fall on a straight line through the origin, and that is what it means for a part to be **ohmic**: its current is proportional to the voltage across it, so that doubling the voltage doubles the current, and the voltage divided by the current, which is the resistance, has the same value at every point.

The slope of the line depends on the resistance. A 100 Ω resistor gives a shallower line, with 0.01 A at 1 V and 0.04 A at 4 V, because the same voltage drives half the current. Ohm's law is therefore the statement that an ohmic part has a straight-line graph, and its resistance is the same wherever on the line it is read.

A part for which the law does not hold can still be used in a circuit, but the voltage divided by the current is then *different* at every point of its graph, and no single value of R can be quoted for it.

diagram.caption: A resistor gives a straight line through the origin. Doubling the voltage doubles the current.

steps.headline: A diode passes current in one direction only

lead.text: A **diode** is a part that lets current through in one direction and blocks it in the other. Its symbol is a triangle pointing the way the current may go, ending in a bar that the current may not cross, and in the figure the battery drives current the way the triangle points, so the arrows run round the loop.

A **light-emitting diode**, or **LED**, is a diode that gives off light while current passes through it, and it is the kind of small indicator light supplied in every Arduino starter kit. Turn the battery round, as in the second view, and the diode blocks the current, so almost none flows and the LED stays dark. For a diode the direction of connection *matters*, whereas a resistor works equally well either way round.
On a new LED the longer leg is the one to connect towards the positive terminal, and the shorter leg towards the negative one.

reveal.text: Almost no current flows and the LED stays dark. Reversing a resistor makes no difference, but reversing a diode turns it from a conductor into a blocker, and the circuit behaves as if it were open.

steps.headline: An LED conducts only past its forward voltage

lead.text: Connected the right way round, an LED still carries almost no current until the voltage across it reaches a threshold, and above the threshold the current climbs steeply. The voltage at which it begins to conduct is its **forward voltage**, about 2 V for a red LED and about 3 V for a blue one, and the first view of the figure shows the red LED's curve staying near zero and then turning sharply upward.

The curve is not a straight line, so an LED is not ohmic. Beside a 200 Ω resistor, whose line rises gently, the LED's curve is almost vertical once it is past its forward voltage: a small increase in the voltage produces a *large* increase in the current.

That steepness is the danger. Past its forward voltage the LED cannot limit its own current, and a battery connected straight across it would drive a current large enough to destroy it within moments. Something else in the loop must decide the current, and the next screen shows what.

diagram.alt: A graph of current against voltage for LEDs. The current stays near zero, then climbs steeply past the forward voltage, about 2 volts for a red LED and about 3 volts for a blue one. A resistor gives a straight line instead.
diagram.caption: An LED's current stays near zero and then climbs steeply past its forward voltage. It is not a straight line, so the LED is not ohmic.

steps.headline: A series resistor sets the current through an LED

lead.text: The something else is a resistor in series with the LED. The same current passes both, and their [[voltage drops|The voltage across one part of a loop, equal to the current times its resistance. Met in 'The voltage across a resistor is the current times its resistance'.]] add up to the battery's voltage, as in any series loop, so with a 5 V battery and a red LED that keeps its 2 V forward voltage, the resistor takes the remaining 3 V.

Ohm's law then gives the current from the resistor alone. 3 V ÷ 300 Ω is 0.01 A, which is 10 mA, while a 600 Ω resistor still has 3 V across it but gives 3 ÷ 600 = 0.005 A, or 5 mA. The LED has *no say* in the current, which is set by the resistor that takes the voltage the LED leaves over, and a larger resistor therefore gives a smaller current and a dimmer light.

To choose the resistor for a wanted current, the same relation is turned round: **R = (supply voltage − forward voltage) ÷ current**, with the current in amperes. A small indicator LED is commonly run at somewhere between 10 mA and 20 mA.

diagram.alt: A 5 volt battery, a resistor and an LED in series with a meter. The LED keeps 2 volts and the resistor takes the other 3 volts. A 300 ohm resistor gives 10 milliamperes and a 600 ohm resistor gives 5 milliamperes.

blocks.text: Raise the voltage across a 100 Ω resistor from 0 to 4 V in steps of 1 V, and the current reads 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03 and 0.04 A, rising by the same amount at every step. Make the same measurement on a red indicator light of the kind supplied in an Arduino starter kit, and the current stays too small to read until the voltage approaches 2 V, after which it climbs so steeply that a further small increase in voltage can destroy the part. **One of these parts keeps its current in proportion to the voltage, and the other does not.**

[[Ohm's law|The current in a loop is the voltage divided by the resistance, I = V ÷ R. Met in 'Current in a single loop'.]] holds only for parts whose resistance stays constant, so it can be used directly on the resistor but not on the light. This lesson looks at how a part of the second kind behaves, and then at the calculation of the resistor that makes it safe to use, which is the commonest job a resistor has in a circuit built from a starter kit.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell an ohmic part from one that is not, say how a diode and an LED behave, and choose the resistor that sets the current through an LED.

recap.keyIdea: Ohm's law fits only ohmic parts; an LED conducts one way and only past its forward voltage, so a series resistor must set its current.

blocks.text: A part is **ohmic** when its graph of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin, as a resistor's is, and then Ohm's law gives its current at any voltage. A diode passes current one way only, and an LED conducts only past its *forward voltage*, with a current that rises steeply beyond it, so the part itself cannot limit the current.

A resistor in series does that job. It takes the voltage the LED leaves over, as the [[voltage drops|The voltage across one part of a loop, equal to the current times its resistance. Met in 'The voltage across a resistor is the current times its resistance'.]] of a series loop must add up to the supply, and the current is then that voltage divided by the resistance, so that **R = (supply voltage − forward voltage) ÷ current**.

transfer.prompt: A 6 V battery is connected across a 200 Ω resistor. Calculate the current in amperes.

questions.onCorrect: 5 ÷ 100 is 0.05, so the current is 0.05 A, and volts divided by ohms leave amperes.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. In Ohm's law the voltage goes on top.
That multiplies the two values, but more resistance should lower the current and not raise it.

questions.prompt: Calculate I = 9 V ÷ 300 Ω, in amperes.
hints: Divide the voltage by the total resistance.
The total resistance is already worked out: 300 Ω.
Work out 9 ÷ 300.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rtotal = 100 Ω + 200 Ω = 300 Ω; I = V / Rtotal = 9 V / 300 Ω = 0.03 A.

questions.onCorrect: 9 ÷ 300 is 0.03, so the current is 0.03 A, the value the two meters read.

misconceptions.feedback: Those values use one resistor alone, 100 Ω or 200 Ω. Both resistors lie in the path, so their total goes underneath.

questions.prompt: Calculate I = 6 V ÷ 150 Ω, in amperes.
hints: Divide the voltage by the resistance.
The voltage is smaller than the resistance, so the answer is less than 1.
Work out 6 ÷ 150. Try 600 ÷ 150 first, then move the decimal point.
questions.onCorrect: 6 ÷ 150 is 0.04, so the current is 0.04 A, small because 150 Ω is a large resistance for a 6 V supply.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage, which puts the numbers the wrong way up. The voltage goes on top.
That multiplies the two values, but a resistor holds the current back, so more resistance cannot raise it.

questions.prompt: A single-loop circuit contains one battery and one resistor. Explain why the current is the same on both sides of the resistor.
hints: Think about how many routes the charge has around this circuit.
Ask what would have to happen to the charge for the two values to differ.
Say what the single path implies about the rate of flow at any two points.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: There is only one path, so the same current passes every point in it. Charge is not used up by the resistor; the resistor limits the rate of flow rather than consuming the charge.

questions.onCorrect: One path, so charge passing one point must pass the next. The resistor limits the rate; it does not use up charge.

questions.prompt: A loop has one battery and one fixed resistor. Which change increases the current?
hints: Write I = V ÷ R and look at which quantity each option changes.
Which options change the voltage, and which change the resistance?
Ask what each option does to the number on top of the division, and to the number underneath.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Raising the supply voltage.

choices.label: Raising the supply voltage
Adding a second resistor along the same path
Replacing the resistor with a larger one
Making the connecting wires longer

questions.onCorrect: More voltage on top of V ÷ R raises the current, whereas more resistance of any kind lowers it.

misconceptions.feedback: A second resistor on the same path adds opposition, so the resistance underneath grows and the current falls.
A larger resistor makes the number underneath V ÷ R bigger, and the current falls.
Longer wire adds a little opposition, so it can only lower the current and cannot raise it.

questions.prompt: A 220 Ω resistor and a 330 Ω resistor are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance, in ohms.
hints: Resistors one after another add their resistances.
Write R total = R1 + R2 with the two given values.
Add 220 and 330.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Rtotal = 220 Ω + 330 Ω = 550 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: 220 + 330 is 550, so the total is 550 Ω, because the charge meets both resistors in turn.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts them. Each resistor adds its own opposition to the path, so the resistances are added.
That multiplies them. The opposition of resistors in series builds up by addition, so 220 + 330 is the total.

questions.prompt: Two unequal resistors are connected in series across a battery. Explain what this does to the current in each resistor and to the voltage across each one.
hints: Start from how many routes the charge has through a series pair.
Decide whether the current can differ between two components on one route.
Then say how the supply voltage is shared between unequal resistances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two resistors sit in a single path, so the same current passes through both. The voltage divides between them, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

questions.onCorrect: One path gives one current. The voltage divides, and the larger resistance takes the larger share.

questions.prompt: A third resistor is added to an existing series circuit, along the same single path. What happens to the total resistance?
hints: Recall how series resistances combine.
A third resistor adds another term to that combination.
Decide whether adding a positive term raises or lowers the total.

acceptedIdeas: it rises by the value of the new resistor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by the value of the new resistor.

choices.label: It rises by the value of the new resistor
It falls below the smallest resistance in the path
It stays the same because the path is unchanged
It becomes the average of the three resistances

questions.onCorrect: Each added resistor adds its own value, so a third one always raises the total.

misconceptions.feedback: A new resistor adds opposition. It can't take the total below what was already there.
The path is longer for the charge now: a third resistor adds to the total.
Series resistances add. An average would be smaller than the sum.

questions.prompt: A resistor carries a current of 0.25 A with 6 V across it. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: Power uses both the current and the voltage.
Write P = IV and substitute the two values.
Multiply 0.25 by 6.
questions.onCorrect: 0.25 × 6 is 1.5, so the resistor transfers 1.5 W.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the voltage by the current, which gives a resistance and not a power.
Adding the two numbers mixes different quantities, since power is their product.

questions.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor has 5 V across it. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: You know the voltage and the resistance. Which quantity is missing for P = IV?
Find the current with I = V / R, then use it in P = IV.
Or use P = V² / R: square the voltage, then divide by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = 5 V / 100 Ω = 0.05 A, so P = IV = 0.05 A × 5 V = 0.25 W. Equivalently P = V² / R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.

questions.onCorrect: With voltage and resistance, V² ÷ R = 25 ÷ 100 gives 0.25 W.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the current, and the power needs the voltage as well.
That multiplies the voltage by the resistance, which does not give a power.
That is the voltage squared on its own. Divide it by the resistance as well.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 20 mA through a component. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: Convert the current to amperes before multiplying.
1 mA is 0.001 A.
Multiply the converted current by the voltage.
questions.onCorrect: 20 mA is 0.02 A, and 0.02 × 9 is 0.18, so the power is 0.18 W.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 20 as if it were amperes. A milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere, so 20 mA is 0.02 A.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the power a resistor dissipates and the energy it transfers.
hints: One of the two quantities depends on how long the circuit runs.
Think about what has to be multiplied by time.
State the relationship between the two quantities in one sentence.

rejectedIdeas: power and energy are the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts. Energy is power multiplied by the time the circuit runs, so a 0.25 W resistor transfers 15 J in 60 s.

questions.onCorrect: Power is the rate of transfer in watts. Energy is power times the time it runs.

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 5 V supply at 15 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The LED keeps its forward voltage. How much of the supply is left for the resistor?
Convert 15 mA to amperes.
Divide the leftover voltage by 0.015.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 5 V − 2 V = 3 V. With 15 mA = 0.015 A, R = 3 V / 0.015 A = 200 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: The resistor takes 5 − 2 = 3 V, and 3 ÷ 0.015 is 200, so the resistor is 200 Ω.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole supply voltage by the current. The LED keeps its forward voltage, so the resistor takes only the rest.
That divides by 15 as if the current were 15 A. Convert 15 mA to 0.015 A before dividing.

questions.prompt: Explain why a light-emitting diode is normally wired with a resistor in series with it.
hints: Think about how sharply the diode's current changes once its forward voltage is reached.
Ask what would set the current if the diode were the only component in the path.
State what the resistor does to the current in the branch.

rejectedIdeas: the resistor makes the diode brighter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Past its forward voltage the diode's current rises steeply for a very small voltage increase, so the diode cannot set its own working current. The series resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current in the branch.

questions.onCorrect: The LED's current climbs steeply past its forward voltage, so a series resistor takes the rest and sets the current.

questions.prompt: State what it means for a component to be ohmic, and give one example of a component that is not.
hints: Consider the shape of a graph of current against voltage.
An ohmic component gives a straight line through the origin.
Name a component whose graph is not a straight line.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An ohmic component keeps the current proportional to the voltage across it, so it has a constant resistance. A diode is not ohmic, because its current climbs steeply once the forward voltage is reached.

questions.onCorrect: Ohmic means current proportional to voltage, so the resistance is constant. A diode is not ohmic.

questions.prompt: A light-emitting diode is connected the wrong way round in a low-voltage direct-current circuit. What happens?
hints: A diode conducts in one direction only.
Think about what the reversed connection does to the current in the branch.
Decide what the learner would observe.

acceptedIdeas: almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark.

choices.label: Almost no current flows and the diode stays dark
The diode lights with the same brightness as before
The current doubles because the path is shorter
The diode lights more brightly and cools down

questions.onCorrect: A diode passes current one way only, so a reversed LED stays dark.

misconceptions.feedback: Reversing a diode matters, because it passes current one way only, so the brightness cannot stay the same.
A shorter path is not the issue. A diode passes current in one direction only, and reversed it blocks.
A reversed diode cannot conduct better. It blocks the current, so there is nothing to make it brighter.

questions.prompt: Two 100 Ω branches are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
hints: Start with the sum of reciprocals.
Substitute 100 Ω for both branches.
Add the two reciprocal terms, then invert the result.
questions.onCorrect: 1/100 + 1/100 is 2/100, so the equivalent resistance is 50 Ω: two equal routes halve the resistance.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the resistances, which is the rule for series. Branches add reciprocals.
That is the sum of the reciprocals, 1/R. Turning it over once more gives the resistance in ohms.

questions.prompt: A 12 V supply feeds two branches, which carry 0.12 A and 0.04 A. What total current does the supply deliver, in amperes?
hints: The supply feeds both branches.
Combine the two branch currents.
Add 0.12 and 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The branch currents are 12 / 100 = 0.12 A and 12 / 300 = 0.04 A. Their sum is 0.16 A.

questions.onCorrect: 0.12 + 0.04 is 0.16, so the supply delivers 0.16 A, the two branch currents together.

misconceptions.feedback: Each of those is a single branch, whereas the supply delivers both branch currents together.
Branch currents are added and not averaged, because the supply provides all of them.

questions.prompt: Why is the equivalent resistance of parallel branches smaller than either branch on its own?
hints: Think about what adding a branch gives charge.
Ask what happens to the total current the supply delivers.
Relate that extra current to the resistance the supply sees.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A second branch gives charge another route, so the supply delivers more current for the same voltage. That is why the equivalent resistance is smaller than either branch.

questions.onCorrect: A second branch is another route, so the supply delivers more current and the resistance it sees falls.

questions.prompt: Two lamps are wired as separate routes across a 6 V battery. What is the voltage across each lamp, in volts?
hints: Look at where each lamp connects. Both have one end on each battery terminal.
Compare each lamp's two ends with the battery's two terminals.
Does the battery's voltage get shared out, or does each lamp connect straight across it?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both lamps connect across the same two battery terminals, so each has the full 6 V.

questions.onCorrect: Each lamp is connected between the same two battery terminals, so each has the full 6 V.

misconceptions.feedback: The voltage is not shared out between branches. Each lamp is connected directly across the battery, so each has all of it.
There is only one battery, and each lamp is connected across it, so the most either lamp can have is the battery's own voltage.

questions.prompt: A resistor carries 0.02 A with 2 V across it. What current does it carry with 4 V across it, in amperes?
hints: Use Ohm's law to find the resistance first.
2 V and 0.02 A give a resistance of 100 Ω.
Now divide 4 V by that resistance.
questions.onCorrect: The resistance is 100 Ω, and 4 ÷ 100 is 0.04, so the current at 4 V is 0.04 A, double the first.

misconceptions.feedback: The current changes when the voltage does. Find the resistance first, then use it at the new voltage.

questions.prompt: A resistor is ohmic. What does its graph of current against voltage look like?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: A straight line through the origin
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A straight line through the origin

choices.label: A straight line through the origin
A curve that bends upwards
A flat line

questions.onCorrect: A straight line through the origin: constant resistance means current proportional to voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: A bend means the resistance changes with voltage. That is not an ohmic component.
A flat line would mean the current ignores the voltage.

questions.prompt: The arrow in a diode's circuit symbol points from left to right. Which way can current go through it?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Left to right only

choices.label: Left to right only
Right to left only
Either way

questions.onCorrect: Left to right only: the arrow shows the one direction a diode passes.

misconceptions.feedback: The arrow points the way the diode passes current, not the way it blocks.
A diode is a one-way component. It does not pass current both ways.

questions.prompt: The voltage across an LED rises slowly from 0 V. What does its current do?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply

choices.label: Stays near zero, then climbs steeply
Rises in a straight line, like a resistor's
Falls as the voltage rises

questions.onCorrect: Near zero, then a steep climb past the forward voltage: an LED does not follow a straight line.

misconceptions.feedback: A straight line is what a resistor does. An LED is different.
More voltage does not lower the current in a forward-biased LED.

questions.prompt: Why does the series resistor get the voltage the LED leaves over?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply

choices.label: The voltages around a series loop add up to the supply
The LED switches the resistor on
Resistors always take 2 V

questions.onCorrect: The drops in a series loop add up to the supply, so the resistor takes what the LED does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The LED does not switch anything on. The drops in a series loop add up to the supply, so the resistor takes what the LED leaves.
The resistor's voltage depends on the supply and on the LED, so it is not fixed at any one value.

questions.prompt: A 9 V battery lights a blue LED with a forward voltage of 3 V at 10 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: The LED keeps its forward voltage. How much of the supply is left?
Divide that leftover voltage by the current, in amperes.
10 mA is 0.01 A. Work out the leftover voltage divided by 0.01.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 9 V − 3 V = 6 V. R = 6 V ÷ 0.01 A = 600 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: The resistor takes 9 − 3 = 6 V, and 6 ÷ 0.01 is 600, so the resistor is 600 Ω.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole 9 V by the current. The LED keeps its 3 V, and the resistor takes only the rest.
That divides by 10 as if the current were 10 A. Convert 10 mA to 0.01 A before dividing.

questions.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2 V runs from a 12 V supply at 25 mA. Calculate the series resistor, in ohms.
hints: Subtract the LED's forward voltage from the supply.
Convert 25 mA to amperes.
Divide the leftover voltage by 0.025.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The resistor takes 12 V − 2 V = 10 V. R = 10 V ÷ 0.025 A = 400 Ω.

questions.onCorrect: The resistor takes 12 − 2 = 10 V, and 10 ÷ 0.025 is 400, so the resistor is 400 Ω.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole 12 V by the current. The LED keeps its forward voltage, so the resistor takes only the rest.
That divides by 25 as if the current were 25 A. Convert 25 mA to 0.025 A before dividing.

questions.prompt: How many litres pass a mark after the narrow section each second?
hints: Where could the water go if the pipe doesn't leak?
If more arrived than left, what would pile up?
Whatever passes the first mark each second must also pass the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nothing leaks and nothing builds up, so 2 litres pass the second mark each second.

questions.onCorrect: 2 litres. Nothing leaks or piles up in a closed loop, so the flow is the same at every mark.

misconceptions.feedback: Water would have to vanish in the narrow part. Where would the missing water go?
The pump keeps pushing, so some water always passes. Think about what the narrow section can and can't do.

questions.prompt: A single loop holds a battery and one resistor. A meter just before the resistor reads 0.05 A. What does an identical meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: Think of the water in the pipe: did the count change after the narrow neck?
Could any charge leave the wire inside the resistor, or be stored there?
Count the routes the charge has around the loop.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One path, so the current is the same on both sides: 0.05 A.

questions.onCorrect: The single path leaves charge nowhere else to go, so every point of the loop passes the same 0.05 A.

misconceptions.feedback: A resistor holds the flow back, but the loop is still carrying current. If the flow stopped at the resistor, charge would have to pile up in front of it, and in a wire it does not.
Half would mean that half of the charge had vanished inside the resistor. Charge is neither created nor destroyed there, so what enters each second also leaves each second.

questions.prompt: Why does Ohm's law divide the voltage by the resistance?
hints: Think about what a bigger resistance does to the flow.
If R grows, should the current grow or shrink?

acceptedIdeas: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current.

choices.label: A bigger resistance holds the current back, so it gives a smaller current
A bigger resistance pushes harder, so it gives a bigger current
Resistance and voltage are measured in the same unit

questions.onCorrect: Dividing by R makes a larger resistance give a smaller current, which is what it means for a part to hold the current back.

misconceptions.feedback: Resistance holds the current back and does not push it. The push comes from the voltage, which is why the voltage is the number on top.
Volts and ohms are different units, and units do not decide where a quantity sits in an equation. What a larger resistance does to the flow does.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives a loop with one 60 Ω resistor. What does a meter just after the resistor read, in amperes?
hints: What does Ohm's law give for the whole loop?
In a single loop the current is the same at every point.
Work out 12 ÷ 60.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = V ÷ R = 12 V ÷ 60 Ω = 0.2 A, and the current is the same on both sides of the resistor.

questions.onCorrect: 12 ÷ 60 is 0.2, so the loop carries 0.2 A, and the same current passes the meter on either side of the resistor.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the voltage by the resistance. A resistor lowers the current, so the answer should be small.
That divides the resistance by the voltage. In Ohm's law the voltage goes on top.

questions.prompt: A 10 V supply drives a single loop containing one 400 Ω resistor. Calculate the current, in amperes.
hints: Which value goes on top in Ohm's law?
Divide the supply voltage by the resistance.
Work out 10 ÷ 400. It is less than 0.1.
questions.onCorrect: 10 ÷ 400 is 0.025, so the current is 0.025 A, which is small because 400 Ω opposes the flow strongly.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. In Ohm's law the voltage goes on top.
That multiplies the two values, but more resistance means less current.

questions.prompt: What does current measure?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

acceptedIdeas: How much charge passes a point each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How much charge passes a point each second

choices.label: How much charge passes a point each second
How much charge is stored in the wire
How hard the battery pushes

questions.onCorrect: Current is a rate: charge passing a point each second, in amperes.

misconceptions.feedback: Current is not stored in the wire. It is charge moving past a point.
How hard the battery pushes is the voltage. Current is the flow that results.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the current?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: V ÷ R

choices.label: V ÷ R
V × R
R ÷ V

questions.onCorrect: Voltage divided by resistance: a bigger resistance gives a smaller current.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying would make more resistance give more current. Resistance holds the current back.
That puts the resistance on top. Ohm's law puts the voltage on top.

questions.prompt: A loop with a 6 V battery and one resistor carries 0.02 A. The resistor is swapped for one with half the resistance. What is the current now, in amperes?
hints: Does halving the resistance make the current rise or fall?
Find the resistance of the first resistor, then halve it.
The first resistor was 300 Ω, so the new one is 150 Ω. Work out 6 ÷ 150.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R = 6 V ÷ 0.02 A = 300 Ω. Half of that is 150 Ω, so I = 6 V ÷ 150 Ω = 0.04 A.

questions.onCorrect: Half the resistance gives twice the current, because the resistance sits underneath in V ÷ R: 6 ÷ 150 is 0.04 A.

misconceptions.feedback: Halving the resistance does not halve the current. A weaker hold-back lets more through, so the current rises.
That is the current before the swap. The resistance has changed, so the current has changed with it.

questions.prompt: A battery gives each coulomb of charge 4 joules. Each second, 0.5 coulombs pass through it. How many joules does the battery deliver each second?
hints: Each coulomb brings 4 joules. How many coulombs pass in one second?
Half a coulomb brings half of 4 joules.
Work out 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each second 0.5 coulombs pass, each carrying 4 J: 0.5 × 4 = 2 J.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5 × 4 is 2, so the battery delivers 2 J every second.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 0.5. Half a coulomb carries less energy than a whole one, so the answer must be smaller than 4.
Adding mixes two different things. Each coulomb carries energy, and that energy is scaled by how many coulombs pass.

questions.prompt: Which resistor transfers more power?
hints: Power uses both current and voltage.
Work out the product for each resistor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They transfer the same power: 0.5 A × 8 V and 2 A × 2 V both give 4 W.

choices.label: The first, with 0.5 A and 8 V
The second, with 2 A and 2 V
They transfer the same power

questions.onCorrect: Both products are 4 W, so neither the current nor the voltage alone shows how hard a part is working.

misconceptions.feedback: It has more voltage but less current. Compare the products and not one number at a time.
It has more current but less voltage. Compare the products and not one number at a time.

questions.prompt: Why can you multiply the current by the voltage to find power?
hints: Think back to the coulombs and joules on the first screen.
What units does the product of coulombs per second and joules per coulomb have?

acceptedIdeas: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second, so the product is energy per second.

choices.label: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
Multiplying always gives the larger of the two numbers
Current and voltage are two names for the same thing

questions.onCorrect: Joules per coulomb times coulombs per second is joules per second, which is watts.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying does not pick out the larger number. What matters is what each quantity measures.
They are different quantities: one counts the coulombs passing each second, the other gives the joules each coulomb carries.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 0.2 A through a lamp for 60 s. How much energy does the lamp transfer, in joules?
hints: Find the power first, from the current and the voltage.
Power is energy each second. How many seconds does the lamp run?
Multiply the power by the 60 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: The power is 0.2 × 9 = 1.8 W, and 1.8 J each second for 60 s is 108 J.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power, in joules each second. The lamp runs for a whole minute, so the energy is larger.
Power is already a rate, so it is multiplied by the time and not divided by it.
That leaves out the voltage. The power has to be found first, from the current and the voltage.

questions.prompt: A 50 Ω resistor carries 0.1 A. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: You know the current and the resistance, not the voltage.
Find the voltage across the resistor with V = IR, or use P = I²R.
Square the current, then multiply by the resistance.
questions.onCorrect: I²R is 0.1² × 50 = 0.01 × 50, so the resistor transfers 0.5 W.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the voltage across the resistor. The power needs one more step, because it is the current times that voltage.
That is the current squared, and it still has to be multiplied by the resistance.

questions.prompt: A heater transfers 100 joules of energy every second. What is its power, in watts?
hints: A watt is one joule each second.
How many joules each second does the heater transfer?
Read the power straight from the joules each second.
questions.onCorrect: 100 W. A watt is one joule each second.

misconceptions.feedback: A watt is one joule each second, so the number is not divided down.
Power in joules each second needs no extra multiplying.

questions.prompt: You know a resistor's voltage and its resistance. Which expression gives its power?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: V² ÷ R

choices.label: V² ÷ R
I² × R
V ÷ R

questions.onCorrect: V² ÷ R. It uses exactly the two quantities you know.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs the current, which you don't have yet.
That is the current, not the power.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery drives 0.12 A through a 100 Ω resistor. A second 100 Ω resistor is wired straight across the same two battery terminals, as a separate route. What total current does the battery supply now, in amperes?
hints: Does the first resistor notice the second? It still has the full battery across it.
Work out the current in the second resistor with Ohm's law.
The battery supplies both routes, so combine the two currents.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each resistor still has 12 V across it, so each carries 0.12 A. The battery supplies both: 0.24 A.

questions.onCorrect: Each resistor keeps its 0.12 A from the full 12 V, and the battery supplies both: 0.24 A.

questions.prompt: A 6 W heater runs for 10 s and a 2 W heater runs for 40 s. How many joules more energy does the 2 W heater transfer?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: E = P × t gives 6 W × 10 s = 60 J and 2 W × 40 s = 80 J, a difference of 20 J.

questions.prompt: A component carries 0.01 A with 1 V across it and 0.04 A with 2 V across it. What is its resistance at 2 V, in ohms?
hints: Resistance is the voltage divided by the current.

Work out 2 ÷ 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At 2 V, R = 2 V ÷ 0.04 A = 50 Ω. At 1 V it would be 1 V ÷ 0.01 A = 100 Ω, so the resistance is not constant.

questions.onCorrect: 2 ÷ 0.04 is 50 Ω, whereas at 1 V the same division gives 100 Ω, so the resistance changes and the part is not ohmic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the resistance at 1 V. At 2 V the voltage divided by the current is different, which is what shows that the part is not ohmic.
That divides the current by the voltage, which turns the relation upside down. Resistance is voltage divided by current.

flashcards.front: What does Ohm's law relate, and how is it written?
flashcards.back: For an ohmic component it fixes the current as the voltage divided by the resistance: I = V / R.

flashcards.front: What does electric current measure, and in what unit?
flashcards.back: The rate at which electric charge passes a point, measured in amperes.

flashcards.front: How is the equivalent resistance of resistors in series calculated?
flashcards.back: By adding them: Rtotal = R1 + R2, and so on for any further resistors in the path.

flashcards.front: In a series circuit, which quantity is the same in every component?
flashcards.back: The current, because a series path does not divide.

flashcards.front: How is the electrical power of a component calculated from its current and voltage?
flashcards.back: P = IV, in watts. Substituting Ohm's law also gives P = I²R and P = V² / R.

flashcards.front: What separates electrical power from electrical energy?
flashcards.back: Power is the rate of energy transfer; energy is that power multiplied by the time the circuit runs.

flashcards.front: Why does a light-emitting diode need a resistor in series with it?
flashcards.back: Its current rises steeply past the forward voltage, so the resistor takes the remaining voltage and sets the current.

flashcards.front: What does it mean to call a component ohmic?
flashcards.back: Its current stays proportional to the voltage across it, so its resistance is constant.

flashcards.front: What happens to equivalent resistance when branches are connected in parallel?
flashcards.back: It falls below the resistance of the smallest branch because the branch conductances add.

flashcards.front: What potential difference does each parallel branch have?
flashcards.back: Each branch has the same potential difference because every branch connects across the same two points.
